If we just randomly combine words (and treat reshufflings of words as equivalent), you could have **8,568** different sentences! :::::::: {.columns} ::::::{.column width="50%"} ::: {.incremental} - It would include real sentences, like: - the dog chased a cat - a squirrel ate some acorns - But it would include _slightly_ wrong sentences, like: - *an cat scratched the tree - *each apple ate the dog ::: :::::: ::::::{.column width="50%"} ::: {.incremental} - And some **very** wrong sentences, like: - *chased cat dog buried the - *acorns dog squirrel tree cat :::: {.fragment} $$ Pk = \frac{n!}{(n -k)!} = \frac{18!}{(13 - 5)!} = 8,568 $$ :::: ::: :::::: :::::::: ## And it misses some real sentences! Randomly combining words and treating reshufflings as equivalent has two other problems: ::: {.incremental} - It would **miss** real sentences like ones you might have created: - the dog chased the cat - some squirrel ate some acorns - Maybe more importantly, it makes a huge error and treats these as the same sentence: - the dog sniffed the cat - the cat sniffed the dog ::: ## Permutations: words can repeat and order matters? So let's say repetitions *are* allowed and we care about the order words appear in. Syntax With just those restrictions, the number of possible sentences drops to **7,776** - This gets ride of most of the ungrammatical sentences, but it leaves us with things like: - *the dog ate a apple - *each squirrel buried a acorns - *an cat scratched an tree How do we fix this? ## Morphology If we add a morphological rule that *an* can only come before words that start with a vowel (apple, acorns) the number of sentences drops to **5,400** and now includes mostly sentences we want it to! Sample sentences look like: - the squirrel sniffed an apple - each squirrel climbed the dog - every squirrel climbed each tree - *the squirrel sniffed each acorns - *the squirrel sniffed every acorns What's wrong? ## Morphology A thing you just know about English without ever having been explicitly told is that *the*, *a*, *an*, *each*, and *every* are singular! They can't be paired with a plural noun like acorns. - If we add a pair of morphological rules that say this, the number of possible sentences drops to **4,056**! - And it's really starting to look like English! - every cat climbed a tree - some cat buried the apple - a tree blocked the squirrel - the squirrel sniffed the apple - each dog chased some acorns ## Morphology? - But we still get sentences like: - *some acorns ate some squirrel - *each apple chased each apple - *an apple climbed a tree - What's wrong with these? ## Semantics! How sentences work ::::: {.incremental} - Speech is a sequence of sounds, that our brains turn into words - Sentences are sequences of words, arranged hierarchically, with morphological, syntactic, and semantic dependencies binding the words together and helping talkers and listeners create meaning - (Looking ahead, we also use social information about the talker to understand speech!) - Sentences are not created by randomly stringing words together - in our play example, only 0.0013% combinations of the possible sentences formed from the 18 words were actually *grammatical* in the linguistic sense ::::: ## How we hear a sentence ::::: {.incremental} - Hearing (and understanding) a sentence involves many, interlocking layers of knowledge, inference, and educated guessing - We use layers of information to predict and understand what others are saying! - One of the ways linguists know for certain that slang, swearing, dialects, and violations of prescriptive rules are valid is that we process these things in the same way! - As listeners, we use our knowledge of sounds, morphemes, syntax, semantics, and pragmatics to create our private, interal representation of what the talker must have meant ::::: ##     if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });

  })();
